newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW - Fed needs dual price/job target - Blinder.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Fed needs dual price/job target - Blinder.

text.p: The Federal Reserve should adopt a dual inflation and jobless rate target to remove uncertainty about its policy goals, former Fed vice chairman Alan Blinder said on Tuesday.
"The Fed should have some combination target, like the core Consumer Price Index and the civilian unemployment rate," Blinder told Reuters.
However, the former Fed vice chairman stressed inflation is the only factor monetary policy can affect on the long run.
Blinder said setting a price target would help the Fed attain its only feasible long-term objective -- fighting inflation.
"Posting a price target -- and that should certainly be a price range -- would remove the mystery about what that target is and would better inform markets," Blinder added.
Asked about current Fed officials' commitment to a target for monetary policy, the former vice chairman said "there is tremendous support for something like that at the Fed."
"The question is 'how explicit do you make it,'" he added.
A Fed source told Reuters the Fed has internally adopted targeting core CPI but has not decided on a time objective.
Blinder stressed announcing a price range target should involve setting a timetable for reaching that target in order to make Fed policy more transparent and credible.

"The Fed should adopt some targets that would be a range for the (inflation) number and also have an arrival date, not in 30 years and not in two months," Blinder noted. "It would be saying 'We'll be getting there over two to four years.'"

The former Fed vice chairman said adopting a dual inflation/jobless rate target would let the Fed pursue its long-term anti-inflation goal while making provisions to help the economy if needed -- but only in the short term.
"What makes the dual target operational is that in the long run, the Fed can only affect inflation, not the unemployment rate," noted Blinder, now a professor of economics at Princeton University.
Blinder pointed out that setting policy to help achieve or maintain maximum employment has always been the Fed's stance and still is -- as per Congress's Humphrey-Hawkins mandate.

"If you look at Fed actions, it's not only about reducing inflation," said Blinder, in reference to the easing of monetary policy in the early 1990s when job creation lagged during the recession and fledgling recovery.
Concern about a possible economic downturn also led the Fed to lower short-term interest rates three times between mid-1995 and the following winter.

The former Fed vice chairman stressed an inflation/jobless rate target would imply "bringing the unemployment rate down to -- but not beyond -- the natural rate" which he favored expressing as the median point in a range.
Blinder equated the natural rate with a jobless rate between 5.3 percent and 5.9 percent.
"I put the natural unemployment rate at 5.6 percent because that's exactly the average for the last two to 2.5 years and inflation is quite stable," the Princeton University professor added.
Blinder, however, cautioned that seeking conditions for maximum employment should be done only if inflation is not running, on the average, above a targeted level.

"Everything being equal, if inflation is running somewhat above the Fed's long-term target for the inflation rate, this should temper the willingness to fight unemployment," Blinder said. "And if inflation is running way above it, this would override it."
"The Fed was extremely correct when monetary policy was very tight (in the 1970s) when inflation was running above 10 percent," he added.
Asked about his assessment of the current monetary policy stance, Blinder described it as "not particularly easy money but not particularly tight money either."
